summary: Describes a SIP event package that carries message-waiting status and message summaries from a messaging system, such as voicemail, to a user's device. This is what lets a phone show a waiting-message indicator.

plainLanguage.summary: It is the little blinking light on a phone telling you that someone left you a message. This document says how the voicemail box tells the phone.

questions: what is sip message waiting indication
what is the message-summary event package
how does voicemail notification work in sip
subtitle: How a voicemail system tells a SIP phone that messages are waiting, and how many, using SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY.

tldr.problem: Phones on traditional networks show a message-waiting light or tone, but SIP's base methods only set up sessions, so an IP phone had no standard way to learn about waiting messages.
tldr.mechanism: A phone subscribes to the message-summary event package, and the messaging system sends NOTIFY requests carrying a small text body of the type application/simple-message-summary, with a yes or no status and optional counts of new and old messages.
tldr.outcome: A phone can show the waiting-message indicator and counts, kept up to date by notifications. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no replacement.

facts.label: Notification rate
facts.value: SHOULD NOT be more than once per second

today: RFC 3842 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata for this RFC lists no obsoleting or updating RFC. It builds on RFC 3265 and RFC 3261.

sections.title: Background and Approach
sections.content:
Message Waiting Indication is a common feature of telephone networks: a special dial tone, a light on the phone, or icons and text. SIP (RFC 3261) was designed for session initiation, and message-waiting status is information orthogonal to a session, so IP phones had no comparable feature.

The RFC solves this with SIP-Specific Event Notification (RFC 3265). A Subscriber User Agent, typically an IP phone, subscribes to the status of its messages. A User Agent acting for the user's messaging system, the Notifier, sends a message summary each time the messages change. A phone can also explicitly fetch the current status.

A User Agent MAY subscribe to multiple accounts, distinguished by Request URI, and multiple User Agents MAY subscribe to the same account. Each phone must first learn of its notifier: by manual configuration on the phone or a proxy, or by discovery using caller preferences (RFC 3841) and callee capabilities (RFC 3840).
sections.plainLanguage: Your phone asks the voicemail box, "tell me whenever something changes." The box then sends a short note each time you get or read a message.

sections.title: The message-summary Event Package
sections.content:
The event package token is message-summary. It defines no event package parameters and no SUBSCRIBE bodies.

Subscriptions MAY range from minutes to weeks. Hours or days are typical and RECOMMENDED, and the default duration is one hour. A notifier MAY shorten the duration to an administrator-defined limit, and SHOULD authenticate the subscription request.

If a SUBSCRIBE has no Accept header, the body type defined here MUST be assumed. A future extension MAY define other NOTIFY bodies.
sections.plainLanguage: The subscription has a name tag, message-summary, and it lasts about an hour unless the phone asks for longer.

sections.title: The Message Summary Body
sections.content:
The body type is application/simple-message-summary, a simple text format meant for machine use, so that low-end phones with no display are not burdened. It starts with a status line, optionally followed by an account line, summary lines and message headers.

  • Messages-Waiting: yes (or no) is the traditional boolean indication.
  • Message-Account: names the account URI. The notifier MUST include it when the subscription is for a group or alias. The URI MUST NOT be in angle brackets.
  • A summary line per message-context-class, such as Voice-Message: 1/3 (0/1): new/old counts, optionally followed by new/old urgent counts in parentheses. Classes come from RFC 3458 (RFC 3458), for example voice, fax, pager, multimedia and text messages.

All counters have a maximum value of 4,294,967,295 (2^32 - 1). Notifiers MUST NOT send a larger value and subscribers MUST treat a larger value as 2^32-1.

A messaging system MAY append RFC 2822 style headers for newly added messages (headers likely to be included are To, From, Date, Subject and Message-ID). These MUST NOT be in the initial NOTIFY, MUST only cover messages added since the previous notification, and the system MUST let an administrator choose which headers are sent. A notifier MUST NOT mark a message old just because it sent a notification.
sections.plainLanguage: The note is a tiny list: is anything waiting, and how many new and old messages of each kind, with a count of the urgent ones in brackets.

sections.title: Subscriber and Notifier Behavior
sections.content:
Right after accepting a subscription, the notifier MUST send a NOTIFY with the current summary, so the subscriber can resynchronize. When the number of new or old messages changes, the notifier SHOULD notify all active subscribers of that account. A messaging system MAY send a NOTIFY with Expires 0 and Subscription-State terminated before a graceful shutdown.

Subscribers typically subscribe for hours or days and re-subscribe well before expiry. If renewal fails, they SHOULD retry periodically with backoff. After expiry, a new subscription MUST use a new Call-ID. Subscribers SHOULD subscribe when a new user logs in, SHOULD renew after a reboot or when connectivity returns, and SHOULD unsubscribe with an Expires of zero when the user de-registers. A subscriber MUST be ready for a NOTIFY at any time, and SHOULD render a valid NOTIFY to the user immediately.

Forked SUBSCRIBE requests are allowed and may install multiple subscriptions. If any Messages-Waiting line says yes, the merged state is yes. To limit traffic, a notifier MAY quarantine rapid changes for seconds or minutes, and SHOULD NOT send NOTIFY requests more often than once per second. Proxies need nothing special beyond forwarding SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY, though they SHOULD allow non-SIP URLs.
sections.plainLanguage: When your phone signs up, the voicemail box immediately tells it the score. After that it only speaks up when something changes, and not more than once a second.

sections.title: Example Message Flow
sections.content:
Section 4.1 walks through Alice's IP phone subscribing to her voicemail gateway for one day (Expires: 86400). The gateway answers 200 OK and immediately sends a synchronizing NOTIFY. In the example, it carries Voice-Message: 2/8 (0/2), meaning 2 new and 8 old messages with none of the new and 2 of the old being urgent.

Later a NOTIFY reports new messages with headers appended, then the phone refreshes the subscription, and finally unsubscribes with Expires: 0 after Alice logs out. Each SUBSCRIBE is answered by a 200 OK and a synchronizing NOTIFY, which is itself answered by 200 OK. The RFC says these examples are informational only.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone signs up, gets the current count, hears about new messages as they come, renews the sign-up, and cancels it when Alice logs out.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
Message summaries and optional message headers are typically very privacy sensitive. At a minimum, subscriptions SHOULD be authenticated and properly authorized. Notifications SHOULD be encrypted and integrity protected, either end to end or hop by hop through SIPS URIs. More detail is in the SIP and SIP Events RFCs.

IANA registrations cover the new event package message-summary and the MIME type application/simple-message-summary. Protocols that cannot carry binary data MUST use a reversible transfer encoding such as base64 for this type, because the format resembles RFC 2822 but is not identical.
sections.plainLanguage: Who has voicemail is private, so the phone should prove who it is and the notes should be sent in a sealed envelope.

messages.note: The subscriber can now ignore it.
